doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Sacred music, Francine and Remo Belli
title: How Duke built the Sacred Concert from older material
summary: Duke reworked tunes over years, such as Come Sunday into David Danced, before assembling his sacred music.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: For Duke, this is one of the works that he reflected on in his autobiography. He referred to his Sacred Concert as the most important music to him. Did he talk a lot about the music before he actually performed it? How did the piece – how was the piece developed for performance?

I think Duke had already started years ago. For example, he took one – he was famous for taking one tune and making it – Harry Carney played the melody. Then a year later, he’d write another arrangement, the same tune, but don’t have Harry Carney. Just have Ray Nance do it. Same tune. In other words, he’s able to get more mileage out of one tune than anybody I ever knew. So what he did with Come Sunday, for example, with the beautiful ballad. He used that for David Danced for Bunny Briggs, where the rhythm section’s playing double-time [Bellson sings this melody while tapping a double-time tempo as accompaniment]. That was an example of what he did with – he wrote that a long time ago. He’d been gathering material off and on for a long time. He finally put the pieces together and made his sacred music.
